label: Complex Numbers as Geometry
notes: This chapter, printed pages 135 to 147, treats the complex plane as a geometric instrument. Every algebraic act becomes a motion, a scale, an angle rule, or a circle-preserving map. We will see addition translate, multiplication rotate and scale, and homographies bend lines into circles.

label: The Argand Diagram
notes: The equation x squared plus one equals zero has no point on the real line, so we enlarge the stage. Writing a number as x plus i y identifies it with the plane point with coordinates x and y. The Argand diagram is the coordinate system in which all later geometry happens.

label: Modulus and Argument
notes: Each nonzero complex number carries two polar coordinates: its modulus r, the distance to the origin, and its argument theta, the angle from the positive real axis. Cartesian form suits addition; polar form suits multiplication, since the product law lives entirely in moduli and arguments.

label: Addition is Translation
notes: Adding complex numbers obeys the parallelogram rule because it is exactly vector addition of position vectors. The difference v equals u plus v minus u recovers the displacement, so subtraction reads off the arrow from one point to another. Addition never touches the polar data of a single multiplier.

label: Multiplication: Rotate and Scale
notes: Multiplying z by a equals r e to the i theta scales z by r and rotates it through theta. The real matrix with columns p, q and minus q, p makes this concrete: its columns are equal length and perpendicular, so the map is a spiral similarity about the origin, never a shear.

label: Similarities of the Plane
notes: Because multiplication is rotation and scaling, every direct similarity of the plane is z maps to a z plus b, fixing the orientation. Conjugating first gives the opposite similarities z maps to a z-bar plus b, which reverse orientation. Together these two families exhaust all similarity transformations of the Argand plane.

label: De Moivre's Theorem
notes: In polar form powers are trivial: r e to the i theta raised to the n equals r to the n e to the i n theta, which is de Moivre's theorem. Moduli multiply and arguments add, so taking a power scales the radius and multiplies the angle by n, turning repeated multiplication into a single geometric rule.

label: nth Roots of Unity
notes: The n solutions of z to the n equals one are the powers of omega equals e to the two pi i over n. They sit on the unit circle at equal angular steps of two pi over n, so they are precisely the vertices of a regular n-gon. The pentagon shows the case n equals five.

label: Euler's Formula
notes: Expanding the exponential series and splitting real from imaginary terms yields e to the i theta equals cosine theta plus i sine theta, so the exponential traces the unit circle. The special case e to the i pi plus one equals zero is a half turn to minus one followed by a return to the origin.

label: The Cross-Ratio
notes: Four complex points have a cross-ratio, a single complex number built from their six pairwise differences. It is real exactly when the four points are concyclic or collinear, so the cross-ratio is the algebraic test for lying on a common circle or line, a fact central to inversive geometry.

label: Mobius Transformations
notes: Linear fractional maps z maps to a z plus b over c z plus d, with a d minus b c nonzero, compose translations, dilative rotations, and inversion. They send generalized circles to generalized circles, preserve the cross-ratio, and are conformal: wherever the derivative is nonzero, local angles are preserved exactly.

label: Geometry by Complex Coordinates
notes: Assigning complex coordinates turns plane theorems into algebra. Equilateral triangles satisfy a clean quadratic relation among their vertices, rotations are multiplications by unit numbers, and concyclicity is a real cross-ratio. The chapter's lesson: choose coordinates where the invariant you care about becomes a single computable expression.
